name: Pattern 4: Hints, Not Answers
title: Pattern 4: Hints, Not Answers
answer: Hints, Not Answers is a pattern for using AI in schools where the tool asks questions and offers clues instead of giving the solution, so that students keep doing the thinking. It matters because a tutor that hands over answers makes practice easier but learning worse, while one that gives hints protects learning.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern comes from the study that opened Chapter 1, which found that answer-giving tutors weaken learning and hint-giving tutors protect it. The idea is to set up any AI product so it asks questions, offers clues, and makes the student try before it helps further. The problem it solves is that most general chat tools will simply supply the answer unless the school configures them otherwise. With a school account in a tool such as Gemini for Education, a teacher can write standing instructions that forbid full solutions and require the tool to ask what the student has tried first. The pattern keeps the struggle with the student, where the learning happens, rather than letting the tool remove it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the early grades, the pattern belongs mostly to the teacher rather than the child. A second grade teacher might use AI to plan a set of guiding questions for a reading group and then ask those questions out loud herself. In high school, students might use a configured tutor for homework, with the conversation log visible to the teacher. Across both, the strongest results in the research came when adults set the tool up carefully and stayed in the room. In the Nigerian trial described in Chapter 1, teachers wrote the opening prompt for every session and walked the room the whole time.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this pattern as growing directly out of the study that opened Chapter 1, which found that a tutor giving answers makes practice easier and learning worse, while a tutor giving hints protects learning (Bastani et al., 2025). It also reports that the strongest results in the research came when adults set the tool up carefully and stayed in the room, and it points to the Nigerian trial described in Chapter 1, where teachers wrote the opening prompt for every session and walked the room the whole time (De Simone et al., 2025). Figure 2.4 is cited as showing the difference between the two kinds of tool at a glance.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Most general chat tools do not follow this pattern on their own, so the school has to configure them, which means the setup decision stays with the school and the teacher. The text places the strongest results with adults who set the tool up carefully and stayed in the room, so supervision is part of the pattern rather than an optional extra. In the early grades the pattern belongs to the teacher, not the child, which keeps young students away from the tool itself. In high school the conversation log stays visible to the teacher, so the student's use is open to review. The choice of when to help further, and how much, remains a human judgment.
